1.pericope_label: Amaziah began to reign at twenty five and did that which was right in the sight of the LORD but not with a perfect heart; when the kingdom was established he slew the servants that had killed his father, but slew not their children, as it is written in the law of Moses

schools.summary: Henry sets out both halves of the verdict together, that the king worshipped the true God, kept the temple service going and countenanced religion in his kingdom, yet did it with no serious piety or devotion of his own and no zeal for the exercises of religion, being no enemy to it but a cool and indifferent friend, a type he finds common in his own day among men who do what is good but not with the heart; he grants that the assassins may have meant to avenge the prophet killed in the previous reign and refuses to let that justify them, since they were not the appointed avengers but presumptuously took God work out of his hands, so that the king did what became him in calling them to account while forbidding the death of their children for their fathers sin; and on the muster he counts the three hundred thousand men against the forces of Jehoshaphat fifty or sixty years earlier, which were four times as many, inferring that sin weakens a people, diminishing them and lessening both their number and their figure, and judges the hiring of Israelites an attempt to make up with money what the kingdom lacked in men, which a word from any prophet, or a glance at what his ancestors got by alliances with Israel, would have prevented, since rashness makes work for repentance.

Clarke reduces the verdict to the arc of the reign, that he began well and soon became an idolater, and pointing forward to the verses where that happens; he also lays out the whole chapter in advance as a scheme of events, the reign begun well, the murderers slain and their children spared, the army reviewed and remodelled, the hired troops dismissed on a prophet expostulation and greatly offended at it, the victory and the prisoners thrown from the rock, the ravaging of the cities of Judah by the dismissed men, the idolatry, the prophet threatened into silence, and the challenge that ends in defeat; Wesley puts the verdict in a sentence, that the man was not an enemy to religion but a cool and indifferent friend, not of serious piety, since his heart was not whole with God.

Ellicott works the verse on the children textually, noting that it coincides almost exactly with the parallel in Kings, that the literal sense is that their sons he put not to death but acted according to what is written in the law in the book of Moses, that the reference is evidently to the command in Deuteronomy which the other book repeats more exactly, and that the closing clause runs, each for his own sin shall they be put to death, where Kings has the singular; on the previous verse he renders the establishing of the kingdom as the confirming of the sovereignty or power to him.

debates.question: What does it mean that he did right but not with a perfect heart?

sides.position: he kept the worship going and countenanced religion without any piety or zeal of his own, a cool and indifferent friend to it
he began his reign well and soon became an idolater, which is the arc the chapter traces

debates.question: Why were the murderers children spared?

sides.position: because the law in the book of Moses forbids it, the reference being to the command in Deuteronomy
because the king did what became him, calling the guilty to account while refusing to punish the innocent for their fathers sin

outliers: Henry alone reads the shrunken muster as evidence of a general decay, that sin diminishes a people and lessens its figure as well as its numbers.
Ellicott alone notes that the closing clause of the law is plural here and singular in Kings.
themes: right done without a whole heart
an avenger who was not appointed
children spared by a written law
an army four times smaller than before

5.pericope_label: Amaziah numbered Judah and found three hundred thousand choice men, and hired a hundred thousand out of Israel for a hundred talents; a man of God bade him send them home, and when he asked what of the hundred talents was told the LORD could give him much more; he smote ten thousand of Seir and cast ten thousand from the rock, and the dismissed troops fell upon the cities of Judah

schools.summary: Gill hears the objection about the money as spoken with some concern, the king being loath to lose so much and knowing there was no demanding it back, and takes the permission that precedes it as irony: if the king will not be advised, let him take them along, exert all his courage and use his military skill, and mark the issue.

Henry sets the objection beside the answer to it, that men often plead against their duty that they are afraid of losing by it, and that a firm belief of God all-sufficiency to make up what we lose in his service makes his yoke easy; he makes the prophet reason practical as well as religious, that troops with whom God was not could not be depended on for service; and on the massacre of the prisoners he calls the act certainly very severe and says we are not told what provocation there was for it.

Clarke quotes the Targum on the prophet reason, that the word of the Lord is not the helper of the Israelites nor of the kingdom of that tribe; Wesley draws the rule in the same words Henry uses, that it is comfortable to employ those who may be hoped to have an interest in heaven and dangerous to associate with those from whom the Lord has departed, calls the permission an ironical concession like bidding a man go and prosper, and gives two grounds for the anger of the dismissed men, the disgrace of the rejection and the disappointment of the spoil, suggesting the hundred talents had probably gone to their officers only, to raise the men.

Ellicott notes that the number mustered falls immensely below the forces of Jehoshaphat and is not much more than half that of Asa, allows the high figures of this book to be suspicious in general while finding a relative propriety here since the country had suffered much in the interval, values the hundred talents at about forty thousand pounds of his own money reckoning four hundred to the talent, and refuses the received sense of the permission, holding that a negative has dropped out of the text so that the prophet means, venture on the expedition by thyself with a good courage, and God will not let thee stumble before the foe, with the next clause rendered, for there is strength in God, to help and to make to stumble; he glosses the dismissal as a sending of the troop to its own place in a heat of anger and judges the anger natural, since the treatment seemed to indicate distrust of their honour and robbed them of the fruits of victory, identifies the rock as Sela, the Edomite capital known to later ages as Petra, allows the savage treatment of the prisoners to be credible in view of the well-known atrocities of ancient warfare though Kings does not mention it, and suspects the name Samaria in the last verse to be corrupt, since otherwise the mercenaries must have gone home first and then set out again by order of the northern king; Keil and Delitzsch call the same total relatively small, gloss the muster as a census of those liable to service from twenty years old and upward, and read the prophet charge as a call to go alone and show himself valiant.

debates.question: Is the prophet permission to go an irony or a promise?

sides.position: an irony, like bidding a man go and prosper: take them along and mark the issue
a promise, since a negative has dropped out of the text: venture by thyself with good courage and God will not let thee stumble
a call to go alone and show himself valiant

debates.question: Why were the dismissed troops so angry?

sides.position: because the treatment implied distrust of their honour and robbed them of the fruits of victory
because of the disgrace and the lost spoil together, the money having gone to their officers only
because men resent what touches their profit or reputation, even when it frees them from trouble

outliers: Ellicott alone emends the prophet sentence by supplying a lost negative, turning a threat into a promise.
Ellicott alone prices the hundred talents in the currency of his own day and weighs the credibility of the chapter numbers.
themes: an army hired and sent home again
a hundred talents weighed against a duty
ten thousand thrown from a rock
a dismissed ally turned plunderer

14.pericope_label: After the slaughter of the Edomites Amaziah brought home the gods of the children of Seir and bowed down to them; the anger of the LORD was kindled and a prophet asked why he had sought gods that could not deliver their own people, and the king bade him forbear, asking whether he were made of the king counsel

schools.summary: Gill makes the point by what the king failed to do, that instead of returning thanks to God for the victory and giving him the glory of it he brought home the conquered gods, and on the king answer to the prophet he grants that the man was no member of the privy council while insisting that he was appointed a counsellor by the King of kings.

Henry calls the idolatry egregious folly and draws the contrast with a later king who at least worshipped the gods of those who had conquered him, where this one worshipped the gods of a people he had himself beaten, who could not protect their own worshippers; he asks what the king saw in them to tempt him and suggests that for the barbarous inhumanity of the massacre he was given up to an idolatry as ridiculous as it was wicked; on the reproof he observes that God sent to convince and reclaim the king before he sent to destroy him and that the prophet reasoned very mildly, from which he draws the rule that men who duly considered the inability of the things they run to when they forsake God would not be such enemies to themselves; and he reads the three moves of the king reply, the taunt that a man had usurped a counsellor place, the silencing, and the threat, noting that the threat seems to remind the prophet of the one killed in the previous reign, so that in menacing this one the king makes himself guilty of both deaths.

Clarke supplies the Targum, which renders the phrase as the idols of the children of Gebal; Wesley hears in the king answer the complacency of a secure sinner who values himself on having silenced his monitors, and replies that it is a plain indication he is marked out for ruin, since those deaf to reproof are ripening fast for destruction.

Ellicott surrounds the act with what is known of the custom and the gods, that the Assyrian inscriptions often refer to carrying off the idols of conquered countries, Esarhaddon recording that he restored the gods of a king of Arabia at that prince entreaty and Assurbanipal that he recovered an image carried off by an Elamite sovereign sixteen hundred and thirty-five years before; he guesses at the motive, that the king may have wished to win the favour of these gods and so keep his hold on what was reckoned their own territory, names the likely candidates from inscriptions and royal names, Hadad, Kosh and Moloch, concedes that the chronicler does portray this king in a darker light than the older account while answering that this proves only the independence of the two, and catches the wordplay that closes the exchange, the prophet taking up the king own word about counsel and implying his own part in a counsel higher than the royal one; Keil and Delitzsch describe the act plainly, that on his return from smiting the Edomites he brought the images of the sons of Mount Seir with him and set them up as gods, giving them religious adoration, and note that the statement is not found in the parallel chapter of Kings, reporting the opinion that it may rest on no definite tradition but be the application to a particular case of a principle generally found at work in the history.

debates.question: Can the report of this idolatry stand beside the account in Kings?

sides.position: it is not in the parallel chapter, and may rest on no definite tradition but be a principle of the history applied to a case
the chronicler does paint the king darker than the older account, but that proves only that the two are independent
the act is of a piece with the man, who was given up to a ridiculous idolatry after the inhumanity of the massacre

debates.question: Why would a victor worship the gods of the beaten?

sides.position: there is no reason in it; it is egregious folly, since those gods could not protect their own worshippers
policy, to win their favour and so keep his hold on what was reckoned their territory

outliers: Ellicott alone brings the Assyrian inscriptions to bear, both on the custom of carrying off a conquered nation gods and on the names of the gods of Edom.
Wesley alone turns the silencing of the prophet into a diagnosis, that a man who congratulates himself on quieting his monitors is marked out for ruin.
themes: a victor bowing to beaten gods
a mild question with an edge
a prophet silenced by a threat
a reproof that names its own fulfilment

17.pericope_label: Amaziah took advice and sent to Joash king of Israel to look one another in the face; Joash answered with the parable of the thistle that courted the cedar and bade him abide at home, but Amaziah would not hear, for it came of God that he might be delivered into their hand

schools.summary: Gill answers the question of whose advice was taken bluntly, not of God nor of his prophets but of some of his nobles like himself.

Henry presses the irony that the prophet was not made of the king counsel, so the king consulted statesmen who would flatter him and bid him go up and prosper, and lays down that those who will not take advice from the word of God will justly be left to the bad advice of men who counsel them to their destruction; he states the explanation that follows as a principle, that the king imprudence was made the punishment of his impiety, God leaving him to himself to act foolishly so that he and his people might be delivered to their enemies because they had forsaken him for the gods of Edom.

Clarke reports the Targum addition after the fable, which turns the parable into a direct charge, that thus had the king done when he sent for a hundred thousand warriors of Israel for a hundred talents and then would not let them go to war but sent them back enraged, so that they spread over the country and cut off three thousand and brought back much spoil. Wesley asks the same question and answers it the same way, that it is good to take advice but it should be of those fit to advise us.

Ellicott renders the challenge itself, let us look one another in the face as combatants do, notes that the counsel taken was a different thing altogether from the counsel the prophet would have tendered, and works the reply word by word, that thou sayest or thou thinkest is added here, that the word rendered Lo may be a corruption of the word for smiting, giving thou hast indeed smitten, and that where this book has a verb meaning to get glory, used so only here, Kings has be honoured and abide at home, the difference being one of vowel points and perhaps due to a copyist; he marks the explanation of the refusal as the chronicler own addition, accounting for the infatuation by the divine predetermination of events.

debates.question: Why would the king not hear the warning?

sides.position: because it came of God, a remark the chronicler adds to account for the infatuation by the divine predetermination of events
because his imprudence was made the punishment of his impiety, God leaving him to himself
because he had taken counsel of flatterers rather than of prophets

debates.question: What does the parable charge him with?

sides.position: presumption, a thistle courting a cedar and trodden down by a passing beast
the specific affront of hiring Israelite troops and sending them home enraged, which the Targum spells out after the fable

outliers: Clarke alone carries the Targum expansion, which drops the figure and names the grievance outright.
Ellicott alone traces the differences between this reply and the one in Kings to vowel points and a copyist.
themes: advice taken from flatterers
a thistle that courted a cedar
a warning refused
infatuation read as judgment

22.pericope_label: Judah was put to the worse before Israel and fled; Joash took Amaziah, broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, took the gold and silver and the vessels in the house of God with Obed-edom and returned to Samaria; after Amaziah turned from the LORD they conspired against him, slew him at Lachish and buried him with his fathers

schools.summary: Henry reads the dating clause of the conspiracy as a connection rather than a date, that from the time the king departed from the Lord the hearts of his subjects departed from him.

Clarke supplies the Targum on the first and last acts, the first when the king walked in the fear of the Lord and the last when he departed from the right way, cites the earlier book for the allotment of the house of collections to the family of Obed-edom, and gives the political reading of the conspiracy, that the king became unpopular once the battle was lost, Jerusalem dismantled and the royal treasures seized, so that the last years of the reign were embittered and he sought safety at Lachish in vain, the man who forsook the Lord being forsaken by every friend; Wesley agrees on the treasure, whose keeping belonged to the posterity of Obed-edom.

Ellicott carries the textual work through to the end, that the Syriac and Arabic omit the verse on Judah being put to the worse, that several Hebrew manuscripts read Ahaziah where our text has Jehoahaz, that the corner gate appears here as the gate that turneth, which would need a word to say which way, that the verb he took has dropped out in an omission old enough to appear in the Greek, and that the closing formula blends this book usual wording with the one customary in Kings; he adds that the clause about Obed-edom is the chronicler own though probably drawn from an ancient document, the name belonging to a Levitical clan, and takes the dating clause as asserting a connection rather than fixing a time, calling attention to the fulfilment of the prophet sentence; Keil and Delitzsch end on the burial place, where the text reads city of Judah against the city of David named everywhere else and given by all the old versions, and explain the slip as a copying error caused by the Judah that follows, which Ellicott calls a transcriber mistake in the same terms.

debates.question: Was he buried in the city of Judah or the city of David?

sides.position: the city of David, as all the old versions have it; the reading here is a copying error caused by the Judah that follows

debates.question: Why did his own subjects kill him?

sides.position: because he had turned from the Lord, the clause being added to assert that connection rather than to fix a date
because he had become unpopular, the battle lost, the wall dismantled and the treasures seized

outliers: Clarke alone gives the fall a political explanation, that the lost battle, the broken wall and the seized treasure made the king unpopular and embittered his last years.
Ellicott alone tracks the chapter closing formula as a blend of this book wording with the phrase customary in Kings.
themes: a wall broken and a treasury emptied
sacred treasure in a Levite keeping
a king pursued to Lachish
one letter that moved a burial place
